I have gathered substantial material from the available sources. Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

---

## Job 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

**Context:** This is the continuation of Eliphaz the Temanite's first speech (begun in ch. 4). Eliphaz argues from personal observation and traditional wisdom that suffering always stems from sin, and that Job must repent to be restored. The chapter ends with Eliphaz's confident assertion that his counsel is proven truth. Yet Job 42:7 records the LORD's rebuke of Eliphaz: "you have not spoken of Me what is right."

---

### v. 1 — "Call out if you please, but who will answer? To which of the holy ones will you turn?"

Eliphaz challenges Job: summon anyone — angelic beings ("holy ones") or godly men — to defend his case. JFB reads it as: "Will God reply to thee?" After the revelation Eliphaz just claimed (ch. 4), Job cannot be so presumptuous as to expect God or any angel to answer his rebellious complaint. Gill notes multiple possible meanings: (a) call upon God in prayer — though Eliphaz implies it would be in vain for a sinner like Job; (b) search through all the saints of history — none match Job's behavior; (c) summon any creature as patron — none will take his side. Ellicott says Eliphaz now becomes "more personal and direct," insinuating Job is "unwise" and "silly." Enduring Word (Guzik) notes Eliphaz appeals to common wisdom: any godly person consulted would agree with him.

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-5/

---

### v. 2 — "For resentment kills a fool, and envy slays the simple."

JFB states that "wrath" and "envy" here refer to fretful and passionate complaints — exactly what Eliphaz charged Job with in 4:5. This is not about God's wrath killing the foolish, but the fool being destroyed by his own resentment. Gill adds that "wrath" could mean either the fool's own passion (some die in fits of rage) or the wrath of the Lord that consumes the wicked. "Envy" (or "jealousy") eats at a person like rot in the bones (Prov 14:30). Eliphaz insinuates Job is this foolish, passionate man. Enduring Word: Eliphaz does not directly accuse Job; he more "suggested that Job do all he could to not be like a foolish man."

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-5.html | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-5/

---

### v. 3 — "I have seen a fool taking root, but suddenly his house was cursed."

Eliphaz appeals to his own observation: "I have seen." He watched a godless man prosper and put down roots, yet suddenly destruction came. JFB: the wicked man spread his root wide in prosperity, but then circumstances arose causing his dwelling to be "cursed" as desolate (cf. Ps 37:35–36). Ellicott: "I cursed" means "I was able to declare distinctly… that his lot would be as follows." Gill: Eliphaz did not wish evil on the man; rather he inwardly recognized that the curse of the Lord was already upon that house (Prov 3:33). The sting for Job: Eliphaz implies Job's devastated household proves he was that fool.

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-5.html

---

### v. 4 — "His sons are far from safety, crushed in court without a defender."

This is a devastating oblique reference to the death of Job's children (the house collapse in 1:18–19). JFB: "crushed in the gate" is a judicial formula — the gate was the place of judgment and public proceedings (Ps 127:5; Prov 22:22). Ellicott offers a different reading: "they crush one another" — internal rivalries and dissensions bring them to ruin, like a house divided against itself. Either way, Eliphaz uses the fate of the fool's children as proof of the father's guilt. Smith's Commentary (StudyLight) is blunt: "Now he's accusing Job of foolishness… because, you see, Job's children were crushed when the house fell."

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/job-5.html

---

### v. 5 — "The hungry consume his harvest, taking it even from the thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth."

The wicked man's harvest is so thoroughly swept away that hungry gleaners will take grain even from among thorns. JFB: even grain hanging on thorn bushes is taken — so complete is the devastation. The second line is better translated "the thirsty" (not "the robber") to match the parallelism with "the hungry." This evokes the Sabean and Chaldean raiders who took Job's livestock (1:14–17). Ellicott suggests an alternative: the wicked man himself eats his own harvest famished, taking it from among thorns — so little is there, and it is choked with thorns.

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html

---

### v. 6 — "For distress does not spring from the dust, and trouble does not sprout from the ground."

Eliphaz argues that trouble does not arise by chance, like a weed randomly springing from soil. JFB: "for truly" — affliction does not come of its own accord; the cause lies with man himself. Gill explains that neither sin nor affliction is a spontaneous product of the earth; both come from man's own evil heart and from God's appointment. Enduring Word: "Trouble does not sprout up like weeds in the field. He was implying that one must sow and cultivate trouble" (Smick).

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-5.html | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-5/

---

### v. 7 — "Yet man is born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward."

Trouble is not random (v. 6); it is the inevitable lot of fallen humanity. JFB: troubles spring from man's common sin by as necessary a law as sparks ("sons of coal") fly upward — troubles are many and fiery (cf. 1 Pet 4:12). Gill connects this to original sin: man is "born to trouble" because he is "born in sin" (Ps 51:5); affliction is the inheritance of Adam's race.

The Hebrew phrase "sons of Resheph" (בְּנֵי רֶשֶׁף) has generated much discussion. Enduring Word cites Andersen: Resheph is a Canaanite god, raising the possibility of "another scrap of imagery from old myths." The Septuagint translated it "young of the vulture"; Jerome rendered it "the bird to flight." But most traditional commentators take it as "sparks" — children of the flame that naturally and necessarily fly upward.

Ellicott finds vv. 6–7 "confessedly very difficult" and proposes a different reading: man is born to labour, but "like sparks of fire, he makes high his flight" — that is, man thwarts his God-appointed lot through pride and presumption, bringing punishment on himself.

Reformed commentator James Montgomery Boice (monergism.com) uses this verse to describe suffering as "simply common to humanity." He likens it to a great bonfire: "each generation is thrown upon the ashes of the generation that went before it." Boice stresses that Job's sufferings were not tied to specific sin — just as Jesus said of the man born blind (John 9:2–3).

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-5/ | https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/articles/onsite/whywouldgod.html

---

### v. 8 — "However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him—"

Having established that trouble comes from God because of sin, Eliphaz now offers advice: seek God and commit your cause to Him. JFB: "Therefore (as affliction is ordered by God, on account of sin), I would have you to seek unto God." Gill calls this good advice in itself — nothing is more proper than to seek God in affliction through prayer, confession, and submission. Yet Enduring Word notes the subtle accusation: Eliphaz "said it tactfully, yet he still said it — that Job was not seeking God and was not committing his cause to God." James Smith (PreceptAustin) comments: "Eliphaz was not in Job's position, and so it was comparatively easy for him to say what he would do. Still, it is the best thing to do."

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-5.html | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-5/ | https://www.preceptaustin.org/job-commentary-james-smith

---

### vv. 9–10 — "the One who does great and unsearchable things, wonders without number. He gives rain to the earth and sends water upon the fields."

Eliphaz launches into a hymn-like praise of God's power. These verses are doctrinally true and beautiful. JFB connects v. 11 to v. 9: God's "unsearchable" dealings aim to raise the humble and abase the proud (Luke 1:52). Enduring Word notes these verses are "a fine example of hymn genre in OT poetry" (Smick), similar to Isaiah 44:24–28. God's power is demonstrated both in nature (rain) and in moral governance. The problem: Eliphaz uses these true doctrines as a weapon against a suffering friend who does not deserve the accusation.

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-5/

---

### v. 11 — "He sets the lowly on high, so that mourners are lifted to safety."

Eliphaz's doctrine: exaltation comes from God alone, not from human striving. JFB says this shows God's "unsearchable" dealings raise the humble and abase the proud — therefore Job ought to humble himself. Ellicott compares the prayer of Hannah (1 Sam 2:6–8) and Psalm 113:7. The implication: if Job humbles himself in repentance, God will lift him up.

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html

---

### vv. 12–13 — "He thwarts the schemes of the crafty… He catches the wise in their craftiness, and sweeps away the plans of the cunning."

These verses describe God's moral governance: He frustrates the cunning and turns their own schemes against them. **v. 13 is quoted verbatim by the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 3:19** with the formula "it is written" — making this the only direct NT quotation from Job (though Rom 11:35 may allude to Job 41:11). JFB notes Paul cites the exact Hebrew, not the Septuagint. The classic illustration is Haman hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai (Esther 5:14; 7:10). Ellicott adds that the word rendered "froward" (KJV) means "crooked, perverse, or tortuous" — the name Naphtali derives from the same root (Gen 30:8). Enduring Word emphasizes the irony: "Great truths misapplied only hurt more those who are already hurting" (Smick).

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-5/

---

### v. 14 — "They encounter darkness by day and grope at noon as in the night."

Judicial blindness sent upon the crafty. JFB: "Judicial blindness often is sent upon keen men of the world" (Deut 28:29; Isa 59:10; John 9:39). Ellicott suggests a possible allusion to the Egyptian plague of darkness (Exod 10:21), noting this as one of several passages in Job hinting at acquaintance with Pentateuchal events, though "too slight for us to be quite sure."

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html

---

### v. 15 — "He saves the needy from the sword in their mouth and from the clutches of the powerful."

God rescues the poor from the "sword" that comes from the mouth of the mighty — i.e., from slander, false accusation, and threatening speech (cf. Ps 57:4; 59:7). JFB and Enduring Word (citing Bullinger) note that "'mouth' is put for the edge of the sword." Ellicott calls this one of the distinctively biblical ideas: "the Lord is thus conceived of and represented, as the Saviour, and the Saviour of them who have no saviour."

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-5/

---

### v. 16 — "So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth."

JFB: the poor have hope of God's intervention, and iniquity is silenced — especially at the last day, through shame (Jude 15; Matt 22:12). Ellicott notes the same phrase "iniquity stoppeth her mouth" appears in Psalm 107:42.

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html

---

### v. 17 — "Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects; so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty."

This is a pivotal verse, likely the original source of Proverbs 3:11–12, which is then quoted in Hebrews 12:5–6. Ellicott notes that the word for "blessed/happy" (אַשְׁרֵי, *ashrei*) is the very first word of the Psalms and appears 25 times there — but this is its **only** occurrence in the entire book of Job.

JFB: the happiness is not in the suffering itself but "the consideration of the righteousness of Him who sends it, and the end for which it is sent." Yet JFB observes Eliphaz "does not give due prominence to this truth, but rather to Job's sin. It is Elihu alone who fully dwells upon the truth, that affliction is mercy and justice in disguise, for the good of the sufferer."

Enduring Word: "With poetic power, Eliphaz emphasized his point that Job's problems are because God corrects His sinful children, and Job is one of those sinful children."

James Smith (PreceptAustin): "To be reproved of God is a comforting evidence of His love and carefulness. Every true child of God desires to have their thoughts, feelings, and ways corrected by their heavenly Father."

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-5/ | https://www.preceptaustin.org/job-commentary-james-smith

---

### v. 18 — "For He wounds, but He also binds; He strikes, but His hands also heal."

An image drawn from wound treatment — God both makes the sore and bandages it. JFB: the healing art in that era "consisted much at that time in external applications." Cross-references include Deut 32:39; Hosea 6:1; 1 Sam 2:6. Ellicott calls this "one of those obvious ones which lose all their force from familiarity with them, but which come home sometimes in sorrow with a power that is boundless, because Divine."

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html

---

### v. 19 — "He will rescue you from six calamities; no harm will touch you in seven."

The "six… yea, seven" formula is a Hebrew numerical proverb pattern (cf. Prov 6:16; Amos 1:3). JFB explains: the idiom fixes on a number (six) to draw attention, then increases force by adding the next higher number (seven, the sacred and perfect number). It means "in all possible troubles," not merely exactly seven. Ellicott observes dryly: "Since evil was emphatically touching Job, the actual irony of these words must have been bitter indeed."

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html

---

### v. 20 — "In famine He will redeem you from death, and in battle from the stroke of the sword."

JFB: "power" (KJV) is literally "hands" — hands are attributed to the sword personified as a living agent. Ellicott notes the tense: "He shall redeem thee" is better read as "He hath redeemed thee" — Eliphaz appeals to what should be Job's own past experience of deliverance as grounds for confidence.

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html

---

### v. 21 — "You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, and will not fear havoc when it comes."

Eliphaz promises protection from slander and from destruction. Enduring Word quotes Adam Clarke: "Perhaps no evil is more dreadful than the scourge of the tongue: evil-speaking, detraction, backbiting, calumny, slander, tale-bearing, whispering, and scandalizing… that member, which is a world of fire, kindled from the nethermost hell."

URLs: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-5/

---

### v. 22 — "You will laugh at destruction and famine, and need not fear the beasts of the earth."

JFB draws a careful distinction: Eliphaz does not mean laughing *in spite of* destruction and famine (as Hab 3:17–18 describes genuine faith doing), but laughing *because* those calamities will not come upon the repentant. The Hebrew word for "famine" here differs from Habakkuk's — here it means the languid state of those lacking proper nourishment (Barnes).

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html

---

### v. 23 — "For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field, and the wild animals will be at peace with you."

JFB: "stones of the field" shall not hurt the fertility of the soil, nor wild beasts the fruits — imagery suited to Arabia-Deserta where stones abounded. The full realization of this promise is yet future (Isa 65:23, 25; Hos 2:18). Ellicott renders it: "For with the stones of the field shall thy covenant be, and the beasts of the field shall be made to be at peace with thee."

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html

---

### v. 24 — "You will know that your tent is secure, and find nothing amiss when inspecting your home."

JFB translates: "Thou shalt rest in the assurance, that thine habitation is the abode of peace; and (if) thou numberest thine herd, thine expectations prove not fallacious" (Umbreit). The Hebrew word rendered "sin" (KJV) literally means "to miss a mark" (as archers in Judg 20:16) — hence "miss nothing" or "find nothing amiss." The word for "habitation" primarily means "the fold for cattle."

Ellicott concurs: "Thou shalt visit thy dwelling-place, and miss nothing."

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html

---

### v. 25 — "You will know that your offspring will be many, your descendants like the grass of the earth."

Ellicott notes the word translated "great" (KJV) means "numerous," which suits the parallelism better. The promise of abundant offspring like grass echoes Psalm 72:16. This is a classic OT blessing for the righteous.

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html

---

### v. 26 — "You will come to the grave in full vigor, like a sheaf of grain gathered in season."

JFB: "full age" — like "full of days" (Job 42:17; Gen 35:29). It denotes not mere length of years but ripeness for death, inward and outward development not prematurely cut short. From the OT perspective, full years were a reward of the righteous (Ps 91:16; Exod 20:12) and premature death the lot of the wicked. JFB adds that the Hebrew "cometh in" is literally "ascends" — the corn is lifted off the earth and carried home; so the good man "is raised into the heap of sheaves" (Umbreit).

Ellicott sees a contrast between going *into* the grave and going *up* to the barn: "The grave in such a case is not the melancholy end of life, but rather the passage to a higher life for which one is already ripe."

Spurgeon preached a sermon on this verse (cited by Enduring Word), developing four points about the Christian's death: (1) Death is inevitable — *You shall come*; (2) Death is acceptable — *You shall come*; (3) Death is timely — *at a full age*; (4) Death is honorable — *as a sheaf of grain ripens in its season*. Spurgeon said: "Even as the color of the wheat is golden… so the gray-headed man has a crown of glory on his head."

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-5/

---

### v. 27 — "Indeed, we have investigated, and it is true! So hear it and know for yourself."

Eliphaz closes with boastful confidence. He claims communal authority: "we have searched it out." JFB: "for thy good" — literally "for thyself." Ellicott: "It is the boastful confidence of Eliphaz which is so hard to bear. He speaks as though Job's experience were as nothing to his."

Enduring Word gathers several important observations:

- **God's rebuke:** "The LORD singled Eliphaz out at the end of the book for a special rebuke" (Job 42:7). Andersen: "Eliphaz's fault is not that his doctrine is unsound; it is his ineptness as a counselor. True words may be thin medicine for a man in the depths."

- **Mason:** "Aspirin is a good and effective medicine. But it is useless against cancer. Similarly, so much of the advice that Eliphaz and the other friends dole out is, in its own right, correct and good and true. But because it is wrongly applied it becomes useless. More than useless, it is a lie."

- **Maclaren:** "The speech ends with a somewhat self-complacent exhortation to the poor, tortured man… Great is authority. An ounce of sympathy would have done more to commend the doctrine than a ton of dogmatic self-confidence."

- **Chambers:** "Preconceptions exist in our own head; if we start out with the preconception that God will never allow the innocent to perish and then we see a righteous man perishing, we will have to say, 'You cannot be a righteous man.'"

- **Smick:** "It is not what Eliphaz knew that is wrong; it is what he was ignorant of — God's hidden purpose — that made all his beautiful poetry and grand truth only a snare to Job."

URLs: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-5.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-5.html | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-5/

---

## Points of Traditional Agreement and Tension

### Broad Protestant Consensus
All major Protestant traditions represented in the consulted sources (Baptist: Gill, Spurgeon; Reformed: JFB, Boice; Anglican: Ellicott; Pentecostal/Charismatic: Guzik/Enduring Word; Methodist/Holiness: Smith via PreceptAustin) agree on the essential reading: Eliphaz speaks theological truth (God disciplines, God restores, God governs justly) but applies it wrongly to Job, who is not suffering for hidden sin. The chapter is a cautionary tale about using true doctrine as a weapon against the suffering.

### Reformed Distinctive
The Reformed sources (JFB, Boice at monergism.org) emphasize divine sovereignty in suffering. Boice treats v. 7 as describing suffering that is "simply common to humanity" — part of God's sovereign ordering of a fallen world, not always tied to specific sin. JFB's note on v. 17 distinguishes Eliphaz's inadequate emphasis from Elihu's fuller development that "affliction is mercy and justice in disguise, for the good of the sufferer."

### Baptist Distinctive
Gill (a Particular Baptist) focuses heavily on original sin in v. 7: man is born to trouble because he is "conceived, shapen, and born in sin." Gill also uses v. 1 to explicitly reject the Roman Catholic appeal to departed saints — "not dead but living ones are meant, and even turning to them is discouraged."

### Lutheran Consideration
No specific Lutheran source (lcms.org, 1517.org) was retrieved in the available searches. The traditional Lutheran reading would align with the cross-and-resurrection pattern seen in v. 18 (God wounds and binds up), viewed through a theology of the cross — God works through suffering, not around it.

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings
No Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) pages were successfully retrieved. The traditional Catholic reading of Job 5 would accord with the general interpretation: Eliphaz's words contain genuine wisdom (the Vulgate preserves the text as Scripture) but his application is flawed. The "holy ones" in v. 1 refers to angels, not departed saints available for intercession — Gill explicitly refutes the Catholic reading on this point.

### Modern Scholarship
The search results from biblehub.com and StudyLight.org note several textual issues:
- The phrase "sons of Resheph" in v. 7 may draw on Canaanite mythological imagery (Andersen, cited by Enduring Word).
- The Septuagint renders "sparks" as "young of the vulture"; Jerome rendered it "bird to flight."
- Peake's Commentary calls v. 15 "undoubtedly corrupt" in the Hebrew, with the usual parallelism wanting.
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary (StudyLight.org) notes the "eloquence, literary skill, sincerity" of Eliphaz's speech while observing its fatal flaw: it is "vitiated by its want of strict correspondence with facts, of which the very case of Job was a crucial instance."
